item.title: The Vanishing Page: AI Firms Scan Then Destroy Rare Book Editions
item.description: AI companies are purchasing physical books in bulk, including rare and out-of-print titles, then using high-speed machines to cut the spines and scan the pages…
item.content:encoded: AI companies are purchasing physical books in bulk, including rare and out-of-print titles, then using high-speed machines to cut the spines and scan the pages before disposing of the originals, according to court documents and industry reports. The process targets pre-2022 books preferred as free of AI-generated content, with services facilitating anonymous bulk orders of up to one million volumes. A federal judge ruled the digitization of purchased books, accompanied by destruction of the physical copies, qualifies as fair use. Anthropic previously conducted a large-scale version of the practice under an internal effort known as Project Panama. The Practice and Legal Background The details resurfaced again after a July 26, 2026, post by the X account @HedgieMarkets described the activity, citing reports of rare books with few surviving copies entering the pipeline. 🦔AI companies are bulk-buying rare books, scanning them through high-speed machines that cut the spines off, and shredding the originals. A service called ISBNdb facilitates orders of up to a million books and keeps buyers anonymous. Pre-2022 books are premium because they're… pic.twitter.com/0YPd8N2oi5 — Hedgie (@HedgieMarkets) July 27, 2026 The post referenced a bookseller’s account to 404 Media and statements from ISBNdb, a company that maintains a large book database and now brokers high-volume acquisitions for AI clients. In a June 2025 ruling in Bartz v. Anthropic, U.S. District Judge William Alsup of the Northern District of California held that digitizing legally purchased print books and using the resulting digital copies to train large language models was fair use. The judge noted that the process replaced the print copies with digital versions without adding new copies or redistributing them. Anthropic later settled related claims involving pirated digital books for $1.5 billion. Anthropic’s Project Panama Court filings unsealed in connection with a copyright lawsuit against Anthropic detailed Project Panama, which began in early 2024. An internal planning document stated that “Project Panama is our effort to destructively scan all the books in the world.” The same document added that “We use a ‘soft codename’ for it because we don’t want it to be known that we are working on this. This document is visible to all Anthropic employees, but you should avoid talking about it in public areas, and the fact that we are working on this should not be shared with anyone outside Anthropic.” Anthropic hired Tom Turvey, the former head of partnerships for Google Books, to obtain books. The company purchased volumes from used-book sellers including Better World Books and World of Books. A vendor proposal referenced converting 500,000 to two million books over a six-month period. The process used a hydraulic-powered cutting machine to remove pages, followed by industrial scanners, after which the physical materials were disposed of or recycled. Role of Brokers and Booksellers’ Reports ISBNdb markets physical books for AI training, stating on its site: “The world’s best AI training data is sitting on a shelf.” It emphasizes that print books from the pre-LLM era are free of AI-generated content. The company facilitates orders ranging from 1,000 to one million books and offers non-disclosure agreements. Its site states that “The optics problem is real. ‘AI company destroys two million books’ is not a headline that generates sympathy.” Booksellers in the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland, and Spain have reported bulk orders for niche and specialized titles. Pieter de Vries of De Vries & De Vries in Haarlem received a request for nearly 3,000 titles from a Singapore-based firm. A German seller noted overnight orders from the Canadian company Zoom Books for unrelated academic works. Dealers stated the purchases did not match typical collector or resale patterns. Destructive scanning is used because it is faster and less expensive than non-destructive methods. The physical originals are eliminated so that only one copy—the digital version—exists at a time, a factor cited in the fair-use analysis. Examples of AI Systems Producing Altered Versions of Established Texts Concerns over the potential for AI tools to rewrite or alter established texts, both fictional narratives and historical accounts, have stressed the valuable role of physical copies as unchanging reference points that cannot be modified digitally. Digital modification of original works is a concerning reality, even if cloaked as efficiency, experimentation, or entertainment. Character.ai, for example, offers a Books feature that permits users to rewrite public domain works such as “Pride and Prejudice” and “Frankenstein” by changing endings, settings, and inserting themselves into the narrative. Researchers at Stony Brook University trained a model to produce a version of “The Great Gatsby” written entirely without the letter “e,” generating text that retains approximate meaning while altering the original wording. A ChatGPT-generated collection titled AI Imagines produced summaries and reimaginations of canonical novels, including “Wuthering Heights,” “Little Women,” and “Jane Eyre,” that omitted major plot elements such as character deaths. Public Discussion No public statements from federal agencies or major education associations specifically addressing the bulk purchase and destruction of physical books for AI training were identified in recent reporting. Library organizations have previously discussed digital preservation challenges and the higher costs of e-book licensing compared with print, but those discussions predate the current reports of industrial-scale destructive scanning. Used-book dealers have expressed concern that uncommon editions with limited surviving copies are being removed from circulation. One anonymous seller told 404 Media that the activity clears inventory while raising questions about the final disposition of rare volumes. Some online commenters have compared the bulk purchase, digitization, and destruction of physical books to themes in George Orwell’s novel “1984,” in which the government systematically alters historical records and written materials to control the official narrative. In the novel, physical documents are destroyed or rewritten so that only the revised version remains, leaving no independent record of the original text. No verified guidance from government bodies, library associations, or industry groups advises individuals to purchase hard-copy books or secure personal copies of favorite titles in response to the reported activity. Still, many readers are choosing to buy and keep physical editions of works they value, treating the printed book as a permanent personal record independent of digital systems. Booksellers have cited the legal precedent established in the Anthropic case as enabling continued acquisition of physical volumes for scanning. Reports indicate the practice extends beyond a single company and includes intermediaries that maintain buyer anonymity.

item.title: Quantum Teleportation Reported in a Qutrit For The First Time
item.description: Earlier this year, we celebrated a first in the field of quantum physics: scientists were able to 'teleport' a qutrit, or a piece of quantum information based…
item.content:encoded: Quantum Teleportation Reported in a Qutrit For The First Time Physics26 December 2019 By David Nield Add ScienceAlert on Google (aleksandarnakovski/iStock) Earlier this year, we celebrated a first in the field of quantum physics: scientists were able to 'teleport' a qutrit, or a piece of quantum information based on three states, opening up a whole host of new possibilities for quantum computing and communication. Up until then, quantum teleportation had only been managed with qubits, albeit over impressively long distances. This proof-of-concept study suggests future quantum networks will be able to carry much more data and with less interference than we thought. If you're new to the idea of qutrits, first let's take a step back. Simply put, the small data units we know as bits in classical computing can be in one of two states: a 0 or a 1. But in quantum computing, we have the qubit, which can be both a 0 and 1 at the same time (known as superposition). Now, the qutrit has the same relationship to the trit, adding superposition to the classical states that can be represented as 0, 1 or 2. A qutrit can be all of these at the same time, making it another jump forward in terms of (for example) computer processing power or the amount of information that can be sent at once. It also adds a level of complexity for quantum computing researchers. Now that we have a grasp on qutrits, what's quantum teleportation? Well, it's getting quantum information from one place to another, through a phenomenon known as quantum entanglement, or "spooky action at a distance", as Albert Einstein called it. That's where two quantum particles (or groups of particles) are interlinked, so that one reveals the properties of the other, no matter how far apart they are in physical terms. It's not actual teleportation in the sci-fi sense, but it is instantly obtaining data from one place based on another reading somewhere else, potentially across a large distance. This quantum information can be beamed via photons of light, and one use we might see in the future is to create unhackable internet networks, protected by the fundamental laws of physics (because any kind of interference would break up the information itself). By splitting the path of a photon up into three parts very close to each other, via a carefully calibrated setup of lasers, beam splitters and barium borate crystals, the researchers were able to create their qutrit and produce a state of entanglement. Over a measurement of 12 states or entanglements, the system produced a fidelity of 0.75 – an accurate result three-quarters of the time. While the setup remains slow and inefficient, it's enough to show qutrit teleportation is possible, the researchers say. The researchers may have been beaten to the line by a separate team though, as Daniel Garisto reports in Scientific American. This second group of scientists only recorded qutrit teleportation across 10 states though, and haven't had their work accepted in a peer-reviewed journal as yet. Whichever set of scientists can truly claim to have got to this new level of teleportation first, it's a significant moment in the field of quantum communications – even if its practical use is limited for now. The team also says they should be able to upgrade their system in the future, perhaps even to the dizzying heights of ququarts (qutrits, with an extra bit added). "Combining previous methods of teleportation of two-particle composite states and multiple degrees of freedom, our work provides a complete toolbox for teleporting a quantum particle intact," write the researchers in their paper. "We expect that our results will pave the way for quantum technology applications in high dimensions, since teleportation plays a central role in quantum repeaters and quantum networks." The research has been published in Physical Review Letters. A version of this article was first published in August 2019.

item.title: Peer-Reviewed Study Confirms Abortion Drug Mifepristone Found in American Drinking Water * The Gateway Pundit * by Cassandra MacDonald
item.description: A newly published peer-reviewed study has found measurable levels of the abortion drug mifepristone in municipal tap water samples collected from three American…
item.content:encoded: Truth Tweet Share Gettr Gab Telegram LinkedIn Free Republic Comments SMS Email Print A newly published peer-reviewed study has found measurable levels of the abortion drug mifepristone in municipal tap water samples collected from three American cities. The research, titled “Anti-Progesterone in Environmental Water,” was authored by Elise Rose, PhD, of the Charlotte Lozier Institute, and Michael Varveris, M.D. The study was published in the July 20 issue of Issues in Law & Medicine. Researchers collected water samples upstream and downstream of treatment facilities as well as from municipal taps in Austin, Texas; Blacksburg, Virginia; and Carbondale, Illinois. The results found significant anti-progesterone consistent with mifepristone in eight of the nine sampling categories, with concentrations reaching as high as 0.041 micrograms per liter, or 41 parts per trillion. Conventional water treatment processes did not consistently remove the compound, and shockingly, in some cases, levels were higher downstream than upstream. The study explains that mifepristone is a synthetic anti-progesterone steroid hormone classified as an endocrine-disrupting compound. Progesterone plays critical roles in fertility, pregnancy, and fetal development. The authors concluded that the presence of this contaminant “could affect the physiology of aquatic animals and human health, including fertility, pregnancy and fetal development,” and called for significant additional investigation into hormones and endocrine disruptors in water sources. Students for Life Action, which inspired and supported the testing effort after commercial labs declined the work, said that the findings validate their work. “A study inspired by Students for Life’s clean water advocacy shows that our concerns are valid,” said Students for Life President Kristan Hawkins. “In three cities where water was tested, the active metabolites of mifepristone, the Chemical Abortion Pill, were in the water. We need the EPA to nationalize this examination, especially in light of so many struggling with infertility. You don’t have to be pro-life to want crystal clear drinking water.” SFLA Executive Vice President Tina Whittington added, “We were told we had to prove mifepristone was in the water in the U.S. to get anyone to care. On our own we started to reach out to water testing companies only to have our business declined. Our frustration became inspiration for this group to find the path to test our drinking water and while we have been vindicated, I hope the larger response is urgency to clean up our water. The harm to endangered species and potentially the human harm is incalculable.” Dr. Rose stated, “Because of the importance of progesterone for human and animal health, the presence of anti-progesterone in environmental and tap water poses potential health risks. Everyone should be concerned that we are possibly being exposed to an endocrine-disrupting compound without our consent.” Medication abortion using mifepristone has become the most common method of abortion in the United States. The study has been submitted to the Environmental Protection Agency for review by its advisory committee. The Gateway Pundit previously reported that on the night of January 25, 2026, surveillance video captured the pair drawing multiple swastikas and profanities in permanent marker across the windows of the ROWT office at 909 E. Rand Road. They specifically targeted a portrait of slain conservative activist Charlie Kirk, born in Arlington Heights and a former volunteer at the local GOP office as a Wheeling High School student, defacing his image. The couple also tossed bags of feces and poured an unknown liquid near the front door. This was no isolated act of random mischief. It came after earlier vandalism in December 2025 that included threatening and offensive messages scrawled into the brick outside the office, specifically and gleefully referencing Charlie Kirk’s wounds. The January attack occurred right before the March primary. ROWT members installed cameras after the prior incident. Despite the use of Nazi symbols against a political organization and the apparent effort to frighten Republican volunteers, the McNerneys were charged only with misdemeanors, not hate crimes. The Daily Herald reported: Cook County Judge Thomas Newinski sentenced the couple to 18 months court supervision, 100 hours of community service, a $100 fine and court costs. Newinski also ordered the couple to pen an apology letter to the Wheeling Township organization. […] Defense attorney Jason Stevens said Thursday that his clients took accountability for their actions, adding that they had no prior criminal record. “They’re going to abide by their sentence,” he said. Many in the Republican community, including ROWT members, point to Illinois’ glaring two-tiered system of justice. Recent cases of Merlin Lu in Cook County and Derek Webb in Lake County saw the accused hit with felony hate crime charges for conduct involving well-recognized symbols of hate. Derek Webb was denied bond; a judge called his actions “extremely troubling” and said they “terrorized” the community. The McNerneys’ case involved the same category of hate symbols, swastikas plastered over Charlie Kirk’s face, yet prosecutors stuck with misdemeanors. No hate crime enhancement. No felony. Just another soft landing in Democrat-controlled Cook County. The victim impact statement submitted by the Republicans of Wheeling Township makes the human cost clear. Supporters are declining to display yard signs for fear their homes will be targeted next. One Jewish member wrote of being “saddened and horrified.” Others described lasting fear of retaliation, reluctance to recruit new members, and the emotional toll of repeated attacks that forced extra police patrols and additional security spending. Despite the notoriety of this case, it has not deterred further attacks. ROWT reported four separate acts of defacement in June alone—two involving sputum deposited on Charlie Kirk’s face and others with offensive notes. A similar note appeared in April. Credit : YourBinCleaning/Instagram (2) NEED TO KNOW Ashton Meyer, 11, launched a trash bin cleaning service in his neighborhood in May to earn extra money The business has since gained more than 100,000 Instagram followers and attracted national attention Ashton plans to expand into seasonal services such as leaf cleanup, snow removal, garden work and lawn mowing A Canadian boy has turned an unpleasant chore into a growing business. Ashton Meyer, who lives in Ontario’s York Region, began going door-to-door in his neighborhood to offer residents a trash bin cleaning service in May, according to CP24. “My dad came up with this business plan because there’s older people on my street,” Ashton, 11, told the outlet. “He said, ‘You should go bring their garbages from their garage to their curb.’ ” Ashton’s dad, Jonathan Meyer, said he saw the chore as an opportunity for his son to build confidence while learning the value of his work. “Plus, it’s a good way to just start putting yourself out there and trying to get some money and learn the value of your time,” Jonathan said. Ashton subsequently launched YourBinCleaning and began approaching neighbors about washing their dirty bins. However, the young entrepreneur admitted that he was initially nervous about getting started and worried that he might not be good at the job. “Then I’m like, ‘Oh, I should do it.’ It’s a good way to make money because … I did not have money,” Ashton said. Ashton said that although rejection can be difficult (he said he cried the first time he received a “no” from a potential client), he no longer lets it discourage him. “When I go door to door, I’m like, ‘I make money off this, these may be my new customers forever and ever,’ ” he explained. Ashton said he now has a customer base of approximately 30 to 40 people. He spends two days each week visiting homes and pitching his service while his father drives him around the neighborhood. He then devotes another two days to cleaning the bins, completing two to three bins per hour. With his mother managing his social media accounts, Ashton has also begun documenting his experience online. The business’s Instagram account, YourBinCleaning, has amassed more than 100,000 followers since the family began posting videos on May 26. Ashton and his father have also appeared on Fox Business to discuss the venture. “We did not expect it to blow up the way it did. We did not get the support that we’ve been getting,” Jonathan told CP24. “I mean, Ashton’s been honored by what happened and people are also paying it forward.” Our new app is here! According to Jonathan, some supporters have donated money to the business, allowing Ashton to begin providing complimentary services to seniors and people with disabilities. The unexpected attention has also created demand for branded merchandise. “People are asking to buy merch from Ashton, so apparently now I have to start packing up T-shirts while I’m driving around,” Jonathan joked. Now He Has Big Plans for the Future Ashton plans to continue working throughout the year by offering different services as the seasons change. “In fall, I’m going to do leaf raking and blowing, and then [in] the winter, I’m gonna get a power broom — I’m gonna save up for one — and I’ll use that power broom and I’ll mow — shovel — the driveways,” he said. “Then in the spring I can do garden cleaning and lawn mowing.” Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE’s free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories. Sermon on Deliverance: What Does It Mean to Be Set Free?
item.description: Few words in the Christian vocabulary carry more weight — or more confusion — than the word deliverance. People search for a sermon on deliverance because they…
item.content:encoded: 🇺🇸 English 🇺🇸 English 🇪🇸 Español Sermon on Deliverance: Dr. Lloyd-Jones on True Freedom Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Few words in the Christian vocabulary carry more weight — or more confusion — than the word deliverance. People search for a sermon on deliverance because they carry the instinct that something is wrong at a level deeper than circumstance. They sense a bondage they cannot name and a freedom they have not yet possessed. The question they are really asking is not merely theological: it is existential. What does it mean to be truly free? Is such freedom actually possible? And if so, by what power and through what means does it come? Dr. Martyn Lloyd-Jones addressed these questions with a precision and pastoral directness that is rare in any era of preaching. Across multiple sermons touching the theme of deliverance — drawn from Luke 4, Romans 8, and Deuteronomy 6 — he mapped the full architecture of human bondage and the full scope of what the gospel of Christ actually accomplishes. His answers are not comfortable. But they are true. And they reach further than most people expect. The Problem Beneath the Problem The first thing Dr. Lloyd-Jones establishes in his sermon on Luke 4:17–19, titled "Deliverance to the Captives," is the diagnosis that most people resist: they do not know they are captives. When Jesus stood in the synagogue at Nazareth and declared He had come to "preach deliverance to the captives," the audience did not celebrate. They were offended. And the reason, Dr. Lloyd-Jones argues, is the same reason the message encounters resistance in every generation: people believe themselves to be free. They have shaken off what they consider the shackles of religion, they are "enjoying the freedom of the world, life, seeing life, living life, having a good time" — and the suggestion that this constitutes captivity strikes them as an insult. But the insult, Dr. Lloyd-Jones insists, is precisely the point. The nature of the bondage Scripture describes is that it is invisible to those under it. This is why the biblical diagnosis of sin does not begin with behavior but with condition. The captive does not feel imprisoned — which is the most dangerous form of captivity there is. The Anatomy of Bondage What, specifically, does Dr. Lloyd-Jones mean by bondage? His sermon on Luke 4 enumerates the forms with clinical specificity: Bondage to the devil. Dr. Lloyd-Jones expounds that all people are born into this world under the dominion of Satan, under the bondage and tyranny of the devil. This is not a statement about dramatic demonic activity. It is a statement about the metaphysical condition of every human being outside of Christ — operating under a governing power they neither recognize nor resist. Bondage to the world. As Paul writes to the Ephesians, all people "in times past walked according to the course of this world." The world has its own gravitational field — its categories of success, its definitions of the good life, its consensus about what matters — and human beings, without regeneration, move entirely within its orbit. Bondage to particular sins. Dr. Lloyd-Jones identifies what Paul calls the "lusts of the flesh and of the mind" — the compulsive patterns of thought and desire that people experience not as choices but as forces. The will, post-Fall, is not neutral. It is bent. Bondage to habit. "Is there anything more difficult than breaking a habit? Oh, how it holds us and binds us." The person who has spent years attempting to break a destructive pattern through willpower and self-discipline knows exactly what this means. Repeated behavior carves neurological grooves; it also carves spiritual ones. Bondage to fear. This may be the most pastoral of the categories Dr. Lloyd-Jones identifies — fear of conscience, fear of the future, fear of death. These are not peripheral anxieties. They are existential conditions that shape how people live, what they avoid, and what they pursue. The cumulative force of this anatomy is that the human being in sin is not merely imperfect or underdeveloped. The bondage is structural, multi-layered, and — crucially — beyond the reach of any merely human remedy. Why Self-Improvement Cannot Deliver This is the point at which Dr. Lloyd-Jones' preaching on deliverance intersects most sharply with the prevailing therapeutic assumptions of modern culture. The popular assumption, in every era, is that human beings are fundamentally capable of self-correction. Education, therapy, medication, social reform, moral resolve — the list of proposed mechanisms is long, and the confidence placed in them is enormous. Dr. Lloyd-Jones does not dismiss the partial goods these things may accomplish. But he is unsparing about their fundamental inadequacy. The barrier between a person and entry into the kingdom of God is sin. Only Christ can take it away. And he delivers from sin not by improving the existing nature but by replacing it — by giving, as Ezekiel 36:26 promises, an entirely new heart. Christ "not only delivers from the guilt and condemnation of sin, he delivers from the power of sin — by giving a new nature." And for the moment a person believes in Christ, the Holy Spirit takes up residence within them and begins working from the inside out. The gospel of Jesus Christ, as Dr. Lloyd-Jones declares in another context, does not improve people. It makes them new. The Spirit of Bondage: A Necessary Precursor In his sermon on Romans 8:15 titled "The Spirit of Bondage," Dr. Lloyd-Jones develops a crucial distinction that the search for deliverance cannot bypass. Before the spirit of adoption comes — the settled assurance of sonship before God — there must first come what Paul calls "the spirit of bondage to fear." This refers to the work of the Holy Spirit in convicting a person of sin. It is the Spirit applying the law, bringing a person to see that God's law is good and holy and spiritual, thereby revealing their own sinfulness, helplessness, and hopelessness before a holy God. This is doctrinally significant. People who search for a deliverance sermon are often looking for relief — and relief is indeed what the gospel ultimately provides. But Dr. Lloyd-Jones insists that there is no genuine deliverance without first a genuine reckoning with the condition from which one is being delivered. The spirit of bondage is not an obstacle to salvation; it is the appointed precursor to it. The Holy Spirit, which dwells in all Christians, is a spirit of truth and always produces a sense of sin and conviction. The Holy Spirit cannot truly lead to God without showing how holy and just Christ is. What this means practically is that the depth of a person's appreciation of deliverance is inseparable from the depth of their recognition of captivity. Those who have never genuinely felt imprisoned will never fully value the act of liberation. Freedom from Fear: What Deliverance Actually Produces In the companion sermon "Freedom from Fear," also drawn from Romans 8:15, Dr. Lloyd-Jones turns to the other side of the equation. The spirit of bondage has a specific and limited role: to awaken the sinner to their desperate condition. Once that work is complete, the spirit of bondage and fear cannot coexist with the spirit of adoption. The former is always replaced by the latter. This is the positive content of deliverance. The person who has been freed from captivity does not merely experience the absence of bondage — they are brought into a categorically new relationship with God. Romans 8:15 is explicit: they cry "Abba, Father." The orphan consciousness is replaced by the consciousness of sonship. Dr. Lloyd-Jones is careful to distinguish this true freedom from what might superficially resemble the spirit of bondage in the Christian life. Depression, spiritual warfare, seasons of doubt — these are real, and he engages them pastorally. The key diagnostic question is how a person responds to Scripture's promises of grace. When someone hears biblical truths about God's love and forgiveness and responds positively — even if temporarily — this reveals that the spirit of adoption is genuinely present. The response to the Word distinguishes the believer in a dark season from the person still under the spirit of bondage. The deliverance Christ accomplishes is not a feeling to be manufactured. It is a status conferred, and a relationship established, that produces — over time and with ongoing sanctification — a settled freedom from the craven fear that once governed the whole person. Deliverance in History: The Pattern of God's Saving Act In "The Call to Liberty," preached at the Fellowship of Independent Evangelical Churches in 1972 from Deuteronomy 6:23, Dr. Lloyd-Jones situates the individual experience of deliverance within the largest possible frame: the entire history of God's dealings with humanity. "The whole history of God's dealing with the human race is nothing but a series of happenings comparable to what we read of in this chapter — God bringing us out always from some bondage." The Exodus from Egypt, the return from Babylon, the Protestant Reformation, the evangelical awakenings — all are instances of the same divine pattern. God identifies His people in captivity. God acts to set them free. And God brings them out not merely to remove them from bondage but to bring them into abundance. Mere separation from wrong is not sufficient for the people of God. God doesn't bring us out merely to bring us out. He doesn't bring us out to leave us in a wilderness. The promised land — the full enjoyment of the gospel's blessings, the assurance of salvation, the satisfaction and joy of knowing God — is the destination. Deliverance is not the terminus. It is the beginning. Dr. Lloyd-Jones also sounds a warning that every person who has tasted freedom needs to hear. The whole tendency of people in sin is to go back into bondage. The impulse toward captivity does not vanish at conversion. Old patterns reassert themselves. The things that enslaved before can be returned to, even after liberation. Eternal vigilance, grounded in Scripture and the ongoing work of the Spirit, is the price of sustained liberty. Listen to Dr. Lloyd-Jones Preach on"Deliverance to the Captives," Dr. Martyn Lloyd-Jones addressed the theme of deliverance across multiple sermons representing different angles of this great biblical truth. All are freely available at MLJTrust.org: "Deliverance to the Captives" — Luke 4:17–19. The anatomy of human bondage and the declaration that Jesus has come to set captives free. "The Spirit of Bondage" — Romans 8:15. Why conviction of sin necessarily precedes the assurance of salvation, and what the Holy Spirit's role is in bringing people to genuine faith. "Freedom from Fear" — Romans 8:15. The positive content of deliverance — the spirit of adoption that replaces the spirit of bondage — and how to distinguish true Christian liberty from its counterfeits. "The Call to Liberty" — Deuteronomy 6:23. God's pattern of deliverance throughout redemptive history, the forms of bondage God's people fall into, and the warning never to return to what they have been freed from. item.content:encoded: Hunter S. Thompson, CIA Gonzo writer Social Influencer of Pseudo-Mockingbird historical events: Peace movement to drug culture Juxtaposition1 Jul 25, 2026 18 1 3 Share Gonzo Journalism (definition): Gonzo journalism is a subjective, first-person style of reporting in which the journalist becomes a central participant in the story, often blurring the line between observer and subject. It rejects the detached objectivity of traditional journalism, instead emphasizing personal experience, emotion, and narrative style. In other words, Gonzo means propaganda, balderdash, mendacity and poppycock. Early “Gonzo journalism” career: After leaving the NATO Air Force, Thompson worked as sports editor for a newspaper in Jersey Shore, Pennsylvania, before relocating to New York City. There, he audited several courses at the Columbia University School of General Studies. During this time, he worked briefly for Time as a copy boy for $51 a week. At work, he typed out parts of F. Scott Fitzgerald‘s The Great Gatsby and Ernest Hemingway‘s A Farewell to Arms to learn the authors’ rhythms and writing styles. In 1959, Time fired him for insubordination. Later that year, he worked as a reporter for The Middletown Daily Record in Middletown, New York. He was fired from this job after damaging an office candy machine and arguing with the owner of a local restaurant, who happened to be an advertiser with the paper. In 1960, Thompson moved to San Juan, Puerto Rico, to take a job with the sporting magazine El Sportivo, which ceased operations soon after his arrival. Thompson applied for a job with the Puerto Rican English-language daily The San Juan Star, but its managing editor, future novelist William J. Kennedy, turned him down. Nonetheless, the two became friends. After the demise of El Sportivo, Thompson worked as a stringer for the New York Herald Tribune and a few other stateside papers on Caribbean issues, with Kennedy working as his editor. After returning to mainland United States in 1961, Thompson visited San Francisco and eventually lived in Big Sur, where he spent eight months as security guard and caretaker at Slates Hot Springs, just before it became the Esalen Institute. At the time, Big Sur was a Beat outpost and home of Henry Miller and the screenwriter Dennis Murphy, both of whom Thompson admired. During this period, he published his first magazine feature in Rogue about the artisan and bohemian culture of Big Sur and worked on The Rum Diary. He managed to publish one short story, “Burial at Sea”, which also appeared in Rogue. It was his first piece of published fiction. The Rum Diary, based on Thompson’s experiences in Puerto Rico, was finally published in 1998 and in 2011 was adapted as a motion picture. Paul Perry notes that Thompson exhibited extreme homophobia while at Big Sur, making violent threats to expel gay bathers from local hot springs. In May 1962, Thompson traveled to South America for a year as a correspondent for the Dow Jones-owned weekly paper, the National Observer. In Brazil, he spent several months as a reporter in Military Intelligence Rio de Janeiro-based Brazil Herald, the country’s only English-language daily. His longtime girlfriend, Sandra Dawn Conklin (later known as Sondi Wright), joined him in Rio. They married on May 19, 1963, shortly after returning to the United States, and lived briefly in Military Intelligence Aspen, Colorado. Sandy was eight-months-pregnant when they relocated to Glen Ellen, Sonoma California. Their son, Juan Fitzgerald Thompson, was born in March 1964. During the summer of that same year, Hunter began taking dextroamphetamine, which is what he would predominantly use for writing until around 1974, when he began to write mostly under the influence of cocaine. Thompson continued to write for the National Observer on an array of domestic subjects during the early ‘60s. One story told of his 1964 visit to Ketchum, Idaho, to investigate the reasons for Ernest Hemingway’s alledged suicide. While there, he stole a pair of elk antlers hanging above the front door of Hemingway’s cabin. Later that year, Thompson moved to San Francisco, where he attended the 1964 GOP Convention at the Cow Palace. Thompson severed his ties with the Observer after his editor refused to print his review of Tom Wolfe’s 1965 essay collection The Kandy-Kolored Tangerine-Flake Streamline Baby. He later immersed himself in the drug and hippie culture taking root in the area and soon began writing for the Berkeley underground paper Spider. Hunter S. item.content:encoded: DARPA's 'ECHO' Project: A Computer System That Declares You've Been 'Exposed' to a Biological or Chemical Threat—With No Physical Evidence Raising questions about how such determinations could be independently verified or challenged. Jon Fleetwood Jul 21, 2026 74 13 19 Share In 2018, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) proposed building a portable computer system allegedly capable of determining whether a person had been exposed to biological or chemical threats—including weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and their precursors. Even with no physical evidence. DARPA outlined the proposal in Broad Agency Announcement HR001118S0023 for a program known as ECHO (Epigenetic CHaracterization and Observation). DARPA proposed accomplishing this by comparing purported changes inside the person’s own biology against a government-built reference library and algorithmically identifying both the alleged threat and when the exposure supposedly occurred. Viewed alongside DARPA’s broader pandemic-era research portfolio, the proposal also raises a larger question explored by this publication’s In Silico Theory: as governments increasingly replace direct observation with computational models, reference libraries, and algorithmic determinations, where does objective evidence end and computer-generated conclusions begin? It also raises an immediate practical question. If an algorithm operating on a government-controlled reference library determines that someone was exposed to a dangerous biological or chemical threat without physical evidence, what meaningful mechanism exists for independently verifying—or successfully challenging—that determination? SAM.gov search results associated with DARPA solicitation HR001118S0023 identify at least $53.8 million in awards, including a $49.2 million contract awarded to the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and a $4.5 million contract awarded to Arizona State University. Message Jon Fleetwood The Core Capability Rather than searching for the biological or chemical agent itself, ECHO proposed “identifying” alleged long-lasting biological signatures left behind after an exposure. DARPA described the objective: “utilize an individual’s epigenome to reveal their history of exposure to weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and WMD precursors.” The solicitation explains why DARPA believed this was possible: “the epigenome is persistent and detectable even when physical evidence has been erased.” That sentence is arguably the centerpiece of the entire program. The proposed system was designed to continue generating exposure determinations long after the original biological or chemical material was no longer available for direct examination. Epigenetics is the study of purported chemical modifications associated with DNA that researchers say can change in response to biological and environmental influences without altering a person’s genetic code. A Government-Built Exposure Library To accomplish that objective, DARPA instructed performers to create what it called the ECHO Signature Panel (ESP)—a centralized library containing purported epigenetic signatures associated with specific exposures. Contractors were required to generate signatures for a minimum of 21 exposure conditions, including mandatory biological threat agents and additional chemical, radiological, explosive, and related materials. Future unknown samples would then be compared against that growing reference panel. DARPA explained the process: “The developed algorithms will need to compare an unknown exposure against the ESP to identify the specific exposure, and when the individual was exposed.” In other words, the proposed system would not simply measure biology. It would compare an individual’s biological patterns against a government-built reference library and output a determination regarding both the nature and timing of an alleged exposure. The Computer Makes the Determination The solicitation envisioned an almost completely automated process. DARPA required: “no human intervention between the time the sample is introduced and results pertinent to exposure and timing is provided.” Insert the sample. Run the algorithms. Receive the determination. The individual would not be interpreting raw laboratory findings. The system itself would produce the conclusion. When the Person Becomes the Evidence Traditional forensic investigations often rely on recovering the biological or chemical agent itself. ECHO proposed something different. According to the solicitation, the system was intended to continue identifying exposure after the physical evidence had been erased by relying instead on computational comparison against stored biological signatures. That architecture raises an obvious question. If the original biological or chemical material no longer exists, and the determination instead comes from an algorithm comparing an individual’s biology against a government-controlled reference library, how would an ordinary person independently verify—or meaningfully challenge—that conclusion? Could the system be weaponized or used fraudulently? The document itself does not answer that question. Instead, it focuses on improving the speed, automation, and reliability of the computational determination. DARPA Anticipated Attempts to Defeat the System One small line buried within the solicitation is especially revealing. Among the categories requiring special handling, DARPA listed: “Potential procedure to evade ECHO Signature Panel identification.” The agency was not merely interested in creating exposure signatures. It was already contemplating how those signatures—and the identification system built around them—might be circumvented. Bottom Line Much of the discussion surrounding ECHO focuses on epigenetics. That risks obscuring what the solicitation actually proposed. At its core, ECHO described a government-built computational system designed to determine whether an individual had been exposed to specified biological or chemical threats by comparing representations of that person’s biology against a centralized signature library—even after the underlying physical evidence was gone. Whether such a system could perform as intended is a separate scientific question. The more immediate journalistic question is what follows if such algorithmic determinations are relied upon in military, intelligence, public-health, or legal settings. When there is no physical evidence and the conclusion rests on a proprietary reference library and algorithmic comparison, what avenues exist for independent verification or meaningful challenge? What happens to the person after the algorithm determines they’ve been exposed? And if those algorithmic determinations are ever used to justify quarantine, criminal investigation, military action, employment decisions, travel restrictions, or other government action, what protections exist for the person the computer has already declared was exposed? item.content:encoded: News & Views How writers are reacting to Substack’s AI transparency tools Honest conversation, the first wave of “How I make this” statements, and an upcoming series on how publishers are using and feeling about AI Jul 24, 2026 1,277 313 141 Share “Spot the difference” by Joro Chen, Brand Designer at Substack Earlier this week, we announced a feature that allows readers to scan text published to Substack to see how much of it is estimated to be written by hand or with AI assistance. We also launched tools for publishers, including the ability to run the program—Pangram—on drafts prior to publication, disable scanning on a post-by-post basis, and add a “How I make this” statement explaining their creative process to set expectations for their readers. These features do not use publisher content, either through Substack or Pangram, to train generative AI models and are now available on web, iOS, and Android. Norms around AI use and its disclosure are unsettled. But we have made the assessment that while the use of AI isn’t necessarily a problem, a lack of transparency around it definitely is. Our aim is to help writers get credit for the work that’s theirs and help their audiences make more informed choices about what they spend their time on. Substack has long been home to brilliant writers and thinkers exploring questions about AI disclosure, making a livelihood through writing, and whether technology can replace human effort in art. Archie Hall, a columnist at The Economist, is highly bullish on AI’s economic upside but recoiled from AI-written prose: “We should shun AI writing even if it is perfectly bearable to read,” he wrote. Science fiction writer Lincoln Michel evangelized intention, and said that AI output can’t be art because it isn’t the product of choices. The Hinternet Editorial Board proposed a Mohs-style scale of AI reliance, from 0 to 10, and Sam Kriss menaced, “If you let AI do your writing, I will come to your house and kill you.” Writers have methodically tested what AI can and can’t generate. Freddie deBoer ran an experiment to track if an LLM could write the parts of a novel that aren’t the prose itself. Engineer, founder, and former venture capitalist Rohit Krishnan tried to measure the statistical signature of literary style, interested to see if a model could eventually learn to write with it. Literature professor Hollis Robbins examined two very different approaches to LLM-generated poetry and asked whether either gets anywhere close to greatness: “For poets, edge cases are the poem.” Elle Griffin wrote a fictional day-in-the-life in a future AI utopia, and Andrea Bartz, the named plaintiff in Bartz v. Anthropic, the case that resulted in a $1.5 billion settlement for writers, wrote her own detailed argument against generative AI today. Writer Teddy (T.M.) Brown named an economic reality rather than a spiritual one—that most commercial writing was never really creative expression to begin with, so what’s disappearing is a livelihood, not a soul: “I am less threatened by the presence of bad writing created by robot-equipped dullards than I am by the specter of there being no way to make a living as a writer at all.” The common thread? We believe that human perspective is an essential ingredient of culture, and this will be true no matter how powerful AI becomes. In the days since the AI scan feature was announced, we’ve seen many publishers putting the tools to use, and initial responses suggest that transparency is the right first step toward protecting writers and improving the experience for their readers. Going forward, you’ll be able to scan posts, replies, and comments on the Substack app to see an estimate of how much of it was written by a human, or with AI assistance. 4:10 PM · Jul 22, 2026 · 54.5K Views 59 Replies · 30 Reposts · 510 Likes Joe Hill@jo3hill Fantastic move from Substack - I reckon this could be the feature of the year! AI is simultaneously: 1. Better at writing than the average person 2. Much worse at writing than professional writers. 3. By virtue of 1, creating lots of slop content which is putting people off of Substack @Substack Today, Substack is launching an AI detection feature, via an integration with @pangram. Going forward, you’ll be able to scan posts, replies, and comments on the Substack app to see an estimate of how much of it was written by a human, or with AI assistance. 5:04 PM · Jul 21, 2026 · 4.47K Views 1 Reply · 4 Reposts · 45 Likes Brie Wolfson@zebriez finally someone upholding the integrity of our feeds Substack @Substack Today, Substack is launching an AI detection feature, via an integration with @pangram. Going forward, you’ll be able to scan posts, replies, and comments on the Substack app to see an estimate of how much of it was written by a human, or with AI assistance. 5:35 PM · Jul 21, 2026 · 6.4K Views 3 Replies · 3 Reposts · 63 Likes Others have raised nuanced concerns about the limitations of labeling and potential downsides for the culture of the community on Substack: the risk of false flags, the limits of what a label can actually capture about a piece of writing, and the potential instinct to scrutinize one another’s process rather than engage with the work itself. AI tool user Monica Hebert wrote a post expressing her concerns about the AI scan, calling it a moral purity test in disguise: A detection tool might estimate whether AI was involved in producing a piece of text. What it cannot tell you is who had the original thought. Who lived the experience. Who spoke the story aloud, rejected the first version, changed the argument, removed the bad language, restored the humor, moved the paragraphs, rewrote the ending, and edited the entire thing again on the Substack page. It cannot tell you who supplied the life. Seventy years old, and using AI. We read all of your feedback, which we take seriously as we continue to evolve the product and host open conversation on this topic. Based on your comments, we made a change yesterday so that publishers can disable scanning on a post-by-post basis without having to scan the post first or interact with Pangram at all. We also know that the use of AI tools is incredibly nuanced, with as many use cases as there are creators on the platform. You can create a “How I make this” statement, visible whenever someone scans a piece of your writing. Many publishers have already drafted their own statements, sharing their views on AI and explaining to their readers how, and whether, they use these tools: “In my writing, the first draft is always mine. I use AI in editing, mostly for clarity. In preparing to write, I often test my ideas against AI and use it to gather background material, including some data analysis and charting that I direct. Any errors or omissions are mine.” —Claudia Sahm “English is not my first language. I use AI as an editor to help me express my thinking in clear, professional English — the way a native-speaking writer would work with a copy editor. It shapes the prose, never the substance.” —Thierry from arvy “No AI to see here darlings!” —Plum Sykes “I use AI throughout my writing process: research, drafting, writing, editing. I typically start with 10-15 min of voice to transcript to capture my thoughts in their raw form, to ensure they are mine. Then I work with a model to draft and iterate until the writing accurately represents my thinking and intent. So, TL;DR if a scan flags this as AI-assisted, that’s accurate and expected.” —Nate “I write gatekept using an open google doc, caffeinated beverages that no longer have any effect on me, and a prayer” —Morgan Vogel “Welcome to The Female Edge. I want to be transparent about how this post was written: every idea here is mine, drawn from my own research, my clinical practice for 30 years, and my six published books. I use AI tools trained on my own writing to help me edit and publish more efficiently, the same way I’d use any other tool in my practice. The framework, models, critical thinking, clinical recommendations, and the care behind it are entirely my own. Thank you for being here.” —Sara Szal MD “I use Claude like an editor uses a team of reporters, which is what I did for most of my career: send them out to gather stories, guide them in how to write those stories up, challenge them on their sources, thoroughly edit their drafts, write their headlines and standfirsts, hit the publish button, and then face the critics (and lawyers) the next day.” —Anthony Lawrance “This involved a lot of hard, human work. Not AI.” —Jim Waterson We’re invested in continuing the conversation. Our aim is to help build trust between you and your readers and create an environment that allows you to make the choices that are right for your creative work and your business. Starting next week, we’ll be kicking off a new series, Model Behavior, featuring top writers, creators, and thinkers addressing this conversation and exploring how they work in the age of AI. And we’d like to continue to hear from all of you: restack, comment, share your “How I make this” statement, or tell us how you think Substack can best support writers and creators as they navigate the muddy waters of AI. 1,277 313 141 Share Previous

item.content:encoded: FILE 001 — APRIL 2026 Tartarian Chronicles Apr 10, 2026 Share # TARTARIAN CHRONICLES ## FILE 001 — APRIL 2026 --- WHAT THE CITIES BUILT UNDERNEATH THEMSELVES *And why the official explanation has never fully accounted for the scale* --- In 1889, the city of Seattle burned to the ground. The official record describes it as an accident. A glue pot, a carpenter's workshop, a fire that spread faster than the volunteer department could contain. Thirty-one blocks of the central business district reduced to ash in eighteen hours. What the official record describes next is what I want you to focus on. Within two years, Seattle rebuilt. But not on the same ground. The city raised its street level by one to two stories — filling in the old ground floor with soil and debris, building new streets on top of the ruins, leaving the original storefronts, sidewalks, and building foundations intact beneath the new city. The reason given: better drainage. The original Seattle had been built too close to sea level. That is a reasonable explanation. It is also incomplete. Because when urban archaeologists and historians began documenting what was left beneath Pioneer Square in the late 20th century — the spaces now marketed as the Seattle Underground — they found something the drainage explanation doesn't account for. The underground wasn't just a buried street level. It was a system. Interconnected passages running between buildings. Brick archways of consistent construction. Ventilation shafts positioned at regular intervals. In several locations, channel infrastructure whose function has never been formally documented. The Seattle city engineering department conducted a partial survey in 1974. The report is available through the municipal archive. It notes, without elaboration, that portions of the subsurface infrastructure predate the 1889 fire by an undetermined period. Predate the fire. Which means the tunnels were not built as part of the post-fire reconstruction. They were already there. --- **THE PATTERN REPEATS** Seattle is not unique. Chicago, 1899. The city authorizes construction of a freight tunnel system beneath the Loop — 60 miles of brick-lined tunnels, 7.5 feet high, running beneath nearly every major building in the downtown core. The official purpose: delivering coal and removing ash from building furnaces without congesting street traffic. The system operated until 1959. Then it was sealed. When engineers surveyed the Chicago tunnel system in 1992 — after a construction accident breached one section and flooded the basements of downtown buildings — they found something the 1899 construction records don't explain. Several tunnel sections showed construction techniques inconsistent with 1899 methodology. Brick laying patterns, arch geometries, and mortar compositions that the survey engineers noted were of an earlier type. The survey recommended further investigation. No further investigation was commissioned. Portland, Oregon tells a version of the same story. The Shanghai Tunnels — a network of passages beneath Old Town — are officially described as routes used by criminal operators to kidnap men for forced labor on sailing ships in the late 1800s. That history is documented and credible. What is less documented is the structural survey conducted by the Oregon Historical Society in 1988. The survey found tunnel sections whose brick dimensions and construction methods did not match any documented construction period in Portland's history. The report used a phrase I have now found in four separate municipal engineering surveys across three cities. *Inconsistent with known construction chronology.* --- **THE QUESTION THE SURVEYS DON'T ASK** Each city has an explanation. Seattle: post-fire reconstruction built over existing drainage infrastructure. Chicago: industrial freight system, fully documented, commercially operated. Portland: criminal network, historically colorful, thoroughly researched. Each explanation accounts for the surface narrative. None of them account for the sections described as inconsistent with known construction chronology. Because if the tunnels predate the documented construction period — if brick dimensions, arch geometries, and mortar compositions point to an earlier methodology than the official record acknowledges — then the question is not who built them for what purpose in the 1880s and 1890s. The question is what was already there when the 1880s builders arrived. --- **WHAT TO LOOK FOR** If you want to verify any of this yourself, these documents are publicly accessible: - Seattle Municipal Archive, Engineering Survey 1974, Subsurface Infrastructure Pioneer Square District - Chicago Department of Transportation, Illinois Tunnel Company records, 1899-1959, Chicago History Museum - Oregon Historical Society, Portland Underground Survey 1988, reference collection The 1974 Seattle report is the most significant. Page 7 contains the notation about predating the fire. It has been sitting in the municipal archive for fifty years. No journalist has cited it. No architectural historian has addressed it in print. No city official has been asked to explain it. The document exists. The question has never been formally asked. That is what this archive is for. --- **NEXT FILE** File 002 examines the water infrastructure beneath three major American cities — systems whose engineering complexity exceeds what the documented construction period should have been capable of producing. On July 16, the Irving City Council approved a zoning change that will allow Tesla to build a hub for its robotaxis at 4203 W. Royal Lane, which is just south of Interstate 635, between Freeport Parkway and Belt Line Road. The vote was 8-0, with Council Member Adam Muller being absent. This case was on a council agenda in May, but the decision was postponed at the request of Irving’s fire and police chiefs, who wanted more time to learn about how they would deal with autonomous vehicles. “Thank you all for putting your confidence and faith in your chiefs and making sure that we’re ready and prepared,” Fire Chief Victor Conley told the council last week. “I appreciate that very much.” (See “Tesla Robotaxis Hub Proposed in North Irving” in Vol. 6, No. 12.) item.description: In the twelfth century, Hildegard von Bingen, a Benedictine abbess in the Rhineland, decided that the existing words were not enough. She had things to name…
item.content:encoded: Hildegard von Bingen: Before Knowledge Was Divided Apr 02, 2026 1 1 1 Share In the twelfth century, Hildegard von Bingen, a Benedictine abbess in the Rhineland, decided that the existing words were not enough. She had things to name that Latin could not quite hold—not mystical things beyond language, but specific things, things with edges and functions and places in an order she could see clearly. So she made new words. She called God Aigonz. She called an angel Zuuenz. From there she built a small vocabulary of several hundred nouns, organized into a list beginning with the divine and moving downward through ranks of being. This is the part of Hildegard’s work that is most disarming, because it is so hard to categorize. It is not quite art, not quite philosophy, and not quite linguistics. The standard interpretation, that Lingua Ignota was a devotional exercise, a secret script, or a kind of private game, never quite satisfies, because the discipline behind it is too evident. She was not playing. She was doing what she did everywhere: insisting on precision. Insisting that the right name for a thing was not a luxury but a necessity, because to name something wrongly was to place it wrongly within the order of things, and the order of things was not decorative. It was structural. It held. She was, by the traditional account, the tenth child of a Rhenish knight, handed over to the Church in infancy as a family tithe—the ecclesiastical ten percent. What kind of mind emerges from that beginning? Not a mystical one, exactly. The impulse behind Lingua Ignota is too orderly and taxonomic, too interested in getting the hierarchy right. Not a scientific one, in any sense we would recognize. Something else: a mind for which naming and knowing were the same act, and for which the failure to name precisely was not an intellectual shortcoming but a kind of damage to the world itself. She had a word for what the damage threatened. She called it viriditas—greenness, vitality, the power of living things to be fully themselves. And if you want to understand Hildegard von Bingen, viriditas is where you have to start, because it is the thread that runs through everything she wrote and composed and built. Without it her work looks like a collection of impressive achievements in separate fields, when it is actually one thing seen from different angles. A Mind Without Disciplines We come to her now through categories she would not have recognized. She appears in histories of medicine, music, mysticism, and of proto-feminism. She appears on reading lists for courses in natural science, theology and in the philosophy of mind. Each of these framings captures something real and misses something essential. The person who emerges from the disciplinary accounts is a kind of medieval polymath, extraordinarily gifted, moving with unusual ease between areas of inquiry that were not yet formally separated. She is admirable, somewhat anomalous, and finally a little mysterious: a mind that seems to exceed its context. But Hildegard did not experience herself as moving between fields. She was not a polymath in the sense of having mastered several distinct disciplines. She was a person for whom the distinctions did not yet exist. Medicine, music, vision, governance, and language were not separate territories she traveled between; they were different expressions of a single truth she was always in the presence of. The mystery is not how she managed to think so broadly. The mystery is what it felt like to think from inside a world where breadth was not an achievement but an assumption, and what we lose when we can no longer imagine that feeling from the inside. Viriditas: The Greening Power Viriditas appears first in her medical writings, in Physica and Causae et Curae, where she describes the living body as a system in constant negotiation with its environment. She does not think of illness as invasion or malfunction. She thinks of it as a slow drift out of proportion, a gradual shift in the balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness that eventually tips the whole system into distress. What causes the drift is not a pathogen but a way of living: poor food, inadequate rest, sustained emotional strain, exposure to harsh conditions over time. The body is not a machine that breaks. It is a process that loses its rhythm. Recovery, accordingly, is less a correction than a restoration. She praises spelt for its capacity to “make good flesh and good blood,” and describes wormwood, taken with cooked wine and honey, as simultaneously checking melancholy, clearing the eyes, strengthening the heart, warming the stomach, and purging the intestines. One plant, one preparation, multiple systems restored at once. The language throughout is one of tendency and balance. What a good remedy does is assist the body in returning to what it already knows how to be. The greening power This is where viriditas enters. She describes it as the greening power: the force that makes a plant push upward through soil in March, that makes a human body repair itself after illness, that makes a community of people living in right relation to one another grow in clarity and purpose over time. It is not a metaphor for biological vitality. It is, in her understanding, the same force operating at different scales. The plant’s green upward push, the body’s return to health, and the community’s moral flourishing are not analogous to one another. They are instances of one thing. If the greening power is real The temptation is to read viriditas as poetic shorthand, a way of gesturing toward connections that Hildegard could feel but not quite explain. That reading is available, but it dissolves the most demanding thing about her work. The distinction between metaphor and claim matters because it determines what counts as medical knowledge. If viriditas is merely a metaphor, if plant growth and human health are similar but separate, then the botanical remedies are interesting folk medicine, the moral claims are theology, and the connection between them is poetic at best. But if viriditas is real, if the greening power actually moves through plants and bodies and communities as a single force, then medicine, moral philosophy, and natural history are not separate inquiries. They are different ways of studying the same phenomenon. For example, to understand how wormwood behaves in the body is to understand something about how vitality flows through living systems. To understand how a community loses its moral clarity is to understand something about how that flow gets interrupted. The disciplines are not separate. They are different angles on viriditas. Hildegard von Bingen’s Music In her musical compositions, the same logic governs a different medium. Her melodies extend far beyond the narrower ranges common in much medieval chant, ascending and descending in long arcs that require sustained control and careful breath management from the singers. She was not composing for ease of performance. She was composing for what the physical discipline of singing teaches the body—and, through the body, the mind. In Ordo Virtutum, one of the earliest surviving musical dramas in Western history, the virtues sing and the devil does not. This is not a theatrical choice. It is a structural argument. Harmony, in her understanding, is what alignment feels like from the inside. When the body is in proportion, when the community is in right relation, when the soul is oriented toward what is true, the result is not just health, peace, or clarity. The result is something like music. And when alignment fails, what you get is not discord but silence: the absence of the capacity to participate in the order that sound both reflects and reinforces. The same argument, made visually Her illuminations make the same argument visually. In the image known as the Cosmic Egg, one of the illustrations from Scivias, concentric rings enclose living forms within luminous boundaries. Flames circle the outer rim. Stars are held within layered bands. Light passes through defined spaces. The image arrives before the text, so you see the order before you read about it, and the sequence is deliberate. Hildegard understood that some things could be shown more precisely than they could be said. Which is why she also understood that the failure of language to name things precisely was not a philosophical problem but a practical one. If the word slipped, the understanding slipped. If the understanding slipped, the practice slipped. And if the practice slipped, viriditas diminished, and things that should have been growing began to wither instead. Governance as Diagnosis This is why the letters matter as much as the medical texts and the musical compositions. She wrote to Emperor Frederick Barbarossa warning him that pride and disorder weaken a realm gradually, eroding its stability through accumulation rather than rupture. She wrote to bishops and abbots in the same language she used to describe melancholy: as a condition that develops slowly, that reverberates through the whole system, that resists correction when it has been allowed to deepen too long. There is something worth pausing on here. Hildegard was not a political theorist, and her letters are not systematic. She was an abbess writing to powerful men, often at their request, and her influence depended entirely on their willingness to receive what she said. Several of them didn’t. Barbarossa, for his part, ignored her warnings and pressed ahead with the schism she had cautioned against. The logic of viriditas did not automatically translate into political persuasion, and pretending otherwise would make her more tidy than she was. What the letters show, even accounting for that, is that she was applying the same diagnostic eye to governance that she applied to the body. Excess, neglect, and imbalance destabilize communities slowly, just as poor diet weakens a body. The deterioration is gradual, the correction requires patience, and the underlying question is always the same: what would allow this system to flourish rather than diminish? What We Lost When Knowledge Was Divided We have no equivalent question. This is the loss that Hildegard von Bingen’s work makes visible, if you look at it from the right angle. The division of knowledge into disciplines produced real gains in narrow domains. But something was also lost, and it is harder to name than the gains, because the loss is precisely the ability to hold things together, to see viriditas as a single phenomenon operating across scales rather than as a family of metaphors that happen to point in the same direction. We can describe the connection between emotional state and physical health, but we describe it as a connection, as a relationship between two things that are otherwise distinct. Hildegard did not describe a connection. She described a single process that expressed itself differently in different media. Lingua Ignota was her attempt to preserve that precision in language, to ensure that the names did not lose their grip on what they were naming as the world grew more complex and the categories multiplied. She failed, in the sense that the language did not survive as a living tongue. But the attempt remains, along with the texts, the music, and the illuminations—a record of what it looked like to hold everything together before we forgot that was possible. 1 1 1 Share

item.content:encoded: House Oversight Committee transparency hearing exposes major CIA ‘mind control’ operation by Jessica Marie Baumgartner July 1, 2026 written by Jessica Marie Baumgartner July 1, 2026 Share 3FacebookTwitterPinterestEmail 2.7K Photo: Alamy Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., led the House Oversight Committee’s hearing on “Mind Control and Accountability: Uncovering the Truth of the CIA’s MKULTRA Experiments” as part of the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets on Tuesday. This revealed the Central Intelligence Agency’s (CIA) destruction of government files related to the experiments and brought witnesses forward to testify regarding the controversial MKULTRA project, which is rumored to have involved giving unknowing participants mind-altering drugs to test their effect on controlling individuals’ behavior. For decades, questions about MKUltra were dismissed or ignored. Today, investigative journalist Tom O’Neill lays out why those questions still deserve answers. @chaosmansonbook WATCH his compelling opening statement below👇 pic.twitter.com/aWJl8CYdKR — Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (@RepLuna) June 30, 2026 During his testimony, investigative journalist Tom O’Neill explained that the 1977 Congressional hearings on the MKULTRA experiments were not a clear representation of what actually took place when the CIA deemed the project a failure. He explained that after being assigned an article exploring the Manson Family Murders where cult members killed complete strangers due to instruction from cult leader Charles Manson, he discovered that a CIA-contracted psychiatrist named Dr. Louis Jolyon West was approached to join a project that would test LSD and other mind-altering drugs on prisoners, hospital patients, and college students without their consent. Although West denied ever getting involved, O’Neill explained that West conducted research at a clinic in San Francisco where Charles Manson and his followers received free medical care. Upon receiving access to hundreds of boxes of West’s records after his death in the 1990s, O’Neill discovered letters between West and CIA leader, chemist Sydney Gottlieb. The first letter was sent from West in 1953, just two months after the CIA authorized the MKULTRA program, and detailed six pages of experiments he conducted that O’Neill said, “could have been written by Josef Mengele,” the infamous Nazi doctor known for inhuman experiments. These details the use of LSD in combination with hypnosis to create confusion, amnesia, and specific mental disorders in people who wouldn’t remember him. “He sought to develop techniques to extract true information, and implant false information in unwilling subjects, and to alter the attitudes and beliefs of quote, previously loyal individuals,” O’Neill stated. Gottleib praised these results and encouraged West’s MKULTRA experiments. In a 14-page report written by West in 1956, he described giving LSD and other drugs with hypnosis to unknowing patients. He claimed to have successfully replaced true memories with false memories in subjects without their knowledge. O’Neill offered to officially enter the documents as proof of his testimony to Congress. WATCH journalist and author Dr. @stephenkinzer’s opening statement at today’s explosive MK Ultra hearing regarding the over classification of secret government programs and the CIA’s quest to weaponize mind control against Americans. pic.twitter.com/UwsSJXWBce — Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (@RepLuna) June 30, 2026 Investigative journalist Stephen Kinzer also shared incriminating information regarding Gottlieb. “In its search for ways to destroy the human mind and body, MKULTRA conducted the most extreme experiments on human beings that have ever been carried out by a U.S. government agency,” he stated. “By any standard, they qualify as medical torture. These experiments took place in prisons, clinics, and safe houses in the United States, in Europe and Asia, and even Latin America.” He explained that in his research he discovered that CIA agents traveled the globe to find “expendables,” people they deemed as disposable for these experiments. “Gottleib had what amounted to a license to kill issued by the U.S. Government.” It’s uncertain how many people were experimented on and how many of them died during the illegal experimentation. Although the investigation into MKULTRA presents many challenges because the project records were destroyed in 1973 after Gottlieb ordered their destruction when he left the CIA, Kinzer urged Congress to unredact the original 1977 hearing records, which were left out at the time due to potential national security threats. He also explained that investigating the 1953 suicide of MKULTRA Dr. Frank Olson could offer more details. “Evidence suggests that his death may not have been a suicide.” “This task force could also consider trying to determine whether some new incarnation of MKULTRA exists today,” he added, noting that advances in AI, cyber technology, and neuroscience have offered covert agencies more tools for mind control experiments worse than MKULTRA. Luna questioned Kinzer about the link between MKULTRA and the 1,600 Nazi scientists who were recruited by the CIA through Operation Paperclip. What does the CIA, Nazi Germany and the Nuremberg Trials all have in common? MK Ultra. I will be meeting with German Parliament tomorrow to identify and locate victims of MK Ultra buried in Germany at the hand of the U.S. government. pic.twitter.com/S9pZtRXHsH — Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (@RepLuna) June 30, 2026 Kinzer stated, “Kurt Blome, who was the chief of biological weapons development for the Nazi government, came to work for the CIA. So did Walter Schreiber, who was the Surgeon General of the Nazi army.” He explained that when researching his book, he discovered the first secret CIA prion/black site prison, where MKULTRA officers worked with Nazi’s to carry out experiments after the Nuremberg Trials. He described them as “Continuations of the experiments that those nazi’s had been conducting just a few years earlier.” The ongoing Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets continues to seek answers regarding the MKULTRA experiments and other mysterious government operations in pursuit of rebuilding public trust between Americans and their government officials.
